title: The Runes
otherNames: futhark (fuþark), from its first six letters
family: Germanic runic alphabets. They are not a learned cipher. Most scholars derive them from a Mediterranean alphabet, most often a North Italic (Alpine) one; the Latin and Greek alphabets are the other candidates.
summary: The runes are the native alphabet of the early Germanic peoples. Inscriptions date them from about 150–200 CE. There are three main rows: the 24-letter Elder Futhark (in use to about 700–800), the Anglo-Saxon futhorc (expanded to 28 or more letters) and the 16-letter Younger Futhark of the Viking Age. Most surviving inscriptions are memorials, ownership marks and messages. A smaller group does seem to be for protection, cursing or healing: bracteate words such as alu and laukaz, the Blekinge curse stones and the Ribe skull fragment. Later, the thirteenth-century Eddic poems and Egils saga present runes as an art of power won by Óðinn. The 18 'Armanen' runes of Guido von List (1908) and most modern rune divination are modern inventions, and the SS took some runes as emblems.

firstAttestation.work: Vimose comb, a bone comb with the runic inscription harja (a name, or a word for 'comb')
firstAttestation.author: anonymous
firstAttestation.locator: National Museum of Denmark, Copenhagen (inventory number not checked)
firstAttestation.notes: Several early objects compete for 'first'. The Meldorf brooch (Schleswig-Holstein, 1st century CE) has four signs that may be runic or Roman; this is disputed. The Svingerud stone (Hole, Norway) was announced in January 2023 by the Museum of Cultural History, University of Oslo. Radiocarbon dating of its cremation grave places it between 1 and 250 CE, which makes it the oldest datable runestone. The first complete row of all 24 runes is on the Kylver stone, Gotland (Rundata G 88, c. 400 CE). Kylver is a limestone slab from a grave at Kylver farm, Stånga parish, found in 1903. Its row ends in a tree-like sign and is followed by the palindrome sueus. The inscription faced into the grave, which is often read as meaning it was meant for the dead, not for readers. That reading is an inference, not a documented fact. No web search was possible for this item: the run's shared search budget was used up before it started. This rests on the compiler's background knowledge of the named work, not on a page read for this brief. Check it against the named edition before publication.

transmission.work: Earliest inscriptions (Vimose comb; Øvre Stabu spearhead, Norway, raunijaz)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: The first securely runic texts, mostly short: names, maker's or owner's words, weapon names.

transmission.work: Kylver stone (Rundata G 88), Stånga, Gotland
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: The first complete futhark row: 24 runes in a fixed order, the earliest evidence that the row was learned as a sequence. On Kylver the row ends …ŋ d o, and the compiler recalls that it puts p before ï; check the order against Rundata.

transmission.work: Gold bracteates (Vadstena, Ög 178; Grumpan, Vg 207; and many others)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Gold pendants modelled on Roman imperial medallions. Some carry futhark rows divided into three groups of eight, the later ættir; others carry short formulas such as alu, laþu, laukaz, auja. These are the centre of the debate on 'rune magic'.

transmission.work: Blekinge stones: Stentoften (DR 357) and Björketorp (DR 360)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Curse formulas in the transitional runic of southern Sweden. They threaten anyone who breaks the monument and name 'runes of power' (ginArunAz) hidden there.

transmission.work: Noleby stone (Vg 63) and Sparlösa stone (Vg 119), Västergötland
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Inscriptions calling runes 'derived from the gods' (raginaku(n)do; rægi[n]kundu). The same formula, reginkunnum, appears in Hávamál 80 centuries later.

transmission.work: Transition to the Younger Futhark (16 runes); Rök stone (Ög 136), early 9th century
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: The row was cut to 16 runes, each covering several sounds, in long-branch ('Danish') and short-twig ('Swedish-Norwegian') forms. Rök, the longest runic inscription, also uses cipher runes.

transmission.work: Ribe skull fragment (Denmark)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: A piece of human skull with a perforation and an inscription naming Ulfr and Óðinn and asking for help against pain and a 'dwarf' (a disease-spirit). It is the clearest early healing charm.

transmission.work: Anglo-Saxon futhorc on objects (Franks Casket, early 8th c.; Ruthwell Cross; Thames scramasax, 9th c., with a full 28-rune row)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: The English expanded the row to 28 runes, and manuscripts go up to about 33, adding ōs, āc, æsc, ȳr, īor, ēar and others. The poet Cynewulf signed four poems (Elene, Juliana, Christ II, The Fates of the Apostles) with runes.

transmission.work: Abecedarium Nordmannicum (St Gallen, Stiftsbibliothek, Cod. Sang. 878); the Alcuin manuscript Vienna, ÖNB Cod. 795 (Gothic letter names)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Learned Carolingian records of runes and rune names. The Vienna codex preserves the Gothic names of the Gothic letters. Those names, with the rune poems, are the basis for reconstructing the Elder names.

transmission.work: Old English Rune Poem (formerly in London, BL, Cotton Otho B.x)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: 29 stanzas, one per futhorc rune, each beginning with the rune name: Christian, gnomic and mnemonic. The manuscript was destroyed in the Ashburnham House fire of 1731. The text survives only in George Hickes's Linguarum veterum septentrionalium thesaurus (Oxford, 1703–05).

transmission.work: Norwegian Rune Poem (Rúnakvæði)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: 16 couplets on the Younger Futhark. Each couplet pairs the rune name with an unrelated proverb. The medieval manuscript burned in the Copenhagen University Library fire of 1728, and the poem survives in 17th-century transcripts (details in Dickins 1915, to verify).

transmission.work: Egils saga Skalla-Grímssonar (attributed by some scholars to Snorri Sturluson; disputed)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Egill carves and blood-reddens runes so that a poisoned horn bursts, carves a curse on a scorn-pole (níðstöng) against King Eiríkr and Queen Gunnhildr, and cures a sick girl by scraping off a botched rune charm and carving a new one. These are literary episodes written about two centuries after the events.

transmission.work: Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (Reykjavík, Árni Magnússon Institute, GKS 2365 4to)
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: Contains Hávamál and Sigrdrífumál. Hávamál 138–145 (Rúnatal) tells how Óðinn hung nine nights on the tree and 'took up the runes', and 146–163 (Ljóðatal) lists 18 charms. Sigrdrífumál lists kinds of runes and where to carve them. Skírnismál 36 threatens a þurs-rune curse. This is the main literary source for rune magic, and it is late and poetic.

transmission.work: Icelandic Rune Poem
transmission.author: anonymous
transmission.what: 16 short stanzas of kennings, each glossed with a Latin word (fé = aurum, Týr = Mars, etc.) and a Norse word for 'chieftain' that alliterates with the rune name.

transmission.work: Johannes Bureus (Johan Bure, 1568–1652), Swedish royal antiquary: runic primers and the manuscript Adulruna rediviva
transmission.author: Johannes Bureus
transmission.what: The first learned 'rune esotericism'. Bureus recorded runestones as an antiquary and also built a Gothicist, Kabbalistic and Hermetic system of 'Adulrunes'. He is the closest point of contact between runes and the Agrippan, Christian-Kabbalist tradition (see Karlsson 2010; Åkerman 1998). The compiler believes, but could not check, that Bureus drew on Agrippa and Reuchlin.

transmission.work: Ole Worm, Runir seu Danica literatura antiquissima (1636); Danicorum monumentorum libri sex (1643)
transmission.author: Ole Worm
transmission.what: Antiquarian publication of runic alphabets and Danish runestones. This is where rune study became Latin scholarship.

transmission.work: Guido von List, Das Geheimnis der Runen (Guido-von-List-Bücherei 1, Vienna)
transmission.author: Guido von List (1848–1919)
transmission.what: Invents the 18-rune 'Armanen' row (fa ur thurs os rit ka hagal not is ar sig tyr bar laf man yr eh gibor). List said it came to him in a revelation during months of blindness after a cataract operation in 1902, and keyed it to the 18 charms of Hávamál's Ljóðatal. It is the root of most völkisch and later occult rune systems.

transmission.work: Völkisch rune occultism and National Socialist use
transmission.author: F. B. Marby, S. A. Kummer, R. J. Gorsleben, K. M. Wiligut; the SS and the Ahnenerbe (founded 1935)
transmission.what: 'Rune gymnastics' and 'rune yoga' (Marby, Kummer) developed out of List. The SS adopted a doubled Sig-rune as its insignia and used the Odal and 'life' runes. Wiligut, Himmler's adviser, designed the SS Totenkopfring with runic signs. Runology in this period was entangled with the regime (Mees 2008; Goodrick-Clarke 1985).

transmission.work: Ralph Blum, The Book of Runes (Oracle Books / St. Martin's Press)
transmission.author: Ralph Blum
transmission.what: A popular rune-casting oracle sold with a set of rune stones. It introduces a blank 'Odin' rune and reorders the row. This is the source of much present-day divinatory rune meaning, and it is modern.

transmission.work: The Unicode Standard: Runic block U+16A0–U+16FF (Unicode 3.0); U+16F1–U+16F8 added in Unicode 7.0
transmission.author: Unicode Consortium
transmission.what: Encodes the Elder, Anglo-Saxon, Younger and medieval runes in one unified block. 7.0 added Tolkien's runes and the Franks Casket variants. The block also has the calendar symbols arlaug, tvímaðr and belgþor (U+16EE–U+16F0), used for golden numbers 17–19 on runic calendars.

claims.claim: The runes were adapted from a Mediterranean alphabet, most probably a North Italic (Alpine) alphabet of the Etruscan family.
claims.evidence: Several letter shapes and the left- or right-running direction match North Italic alphabets. Ludvig Wimmer (1874) argued for Latin; Sophus Bugge and Otto von Friesen argued for Greek, which the dates make hard to sustain. The North Italic thesis (Marstrander 1928 and later) is the most widely held, but there is no consensus.

claims.claim: The word 'rune' meant 'secret, mystery' before it meant 'letter'.
claims.evidence: Gothic rūna translates Greek mystērion in Wulfila's Bible (e.g. Mark 4:11). Old English rūn means 'secret, counsel, whisper', and Old Irish rún, a Celtic cognate, means 'secret'. This is lexical evidence only. It does not show that the letters were themselves secret or magical.

claims.claim: Óðinn won the runes by hanging nine nights on a wind-swept tree, wounded by a spear and 'given to Óðinn, myself to myself'.
claims.evidence: Hávamál 138–139 in the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270). The poem is the only witness. Its date of composition is unknown, and it was written down in Christian Iceland.

claims.claim: Runes were held to be of divine origin.
claims.evidence: Some carvers say so themselves. Noleby stone (Vg 63, c. 600): runo fahi raginakudo, 'I paint/write the rune derived from the gods'. Sparlösa (Vg 119, c. 800): rúnaR … rægi[n]kundu. Hávamál 80 later uses the same word: rúnum … reginkunnum. The belief is documented; the origin itself is legend.

claims.claim: The word alu, frequent on bracteates and other early objects, is a magical or protective formula.
claims.evidence: alu appears alone or in formulas on many 5th–6th-century bracteates, on the Elgesem stone (Norway), on the Lindholm amulet (Skåne), and stamped on cremation urns at Spong Hill, Norfolk. Proposed meanings include 'ale' (Old Norse ǫl, Old English ealu, perhaps a ritual drink), 'protection' or 'sanctuary' (compare Gothic alhs 'temple'), and a link to Hittite words for 'bewitched' (Polomé). Most runologists accept that it was a cultic or amuletic word but do not agree on its sense.

claims.claim: The word laukaz 'leek' on bracteates is a fertility or prosperity charm.
claims.evidence: laukaz and abbreviations of it occur on many bracteates. The Fløksand scraper (Norway) reads lina laukaz, 'linen [and] leek'. Two literary parallels are cited. In Völsa þáttr (Flateyjarbók, 1387–94) a preserved horse-phallus is wrapped in linen and leeks. Sigrdrífumál 8 tells the reader to throw a leek into the cup against poison. Egill's verse calls the sick girl 'linden of leeks'. That the word worked as a charm is an interpretation; that it was written on amulets is documented.

claims.claim: Futhark rows written out on objects (Kylver, the Vadstena and Grumpan bracteates) were magical in purpose.
claims.evidence: Some scholars read a complete row as an amulet, like Latin abecedaria on late-antique amulets. Others read it as a writing exercise or a display of literacy. Kylver's grave context (inscription facing inward) supports the first reading for that stone only.

claims.claim: Runes were used for curses on monuments.
claims.evidence: Björketorp (DR 360) and Stentoften (DR 357) threaten whoever breaks the stone. In the compiler's paraphrase of Björketorp: 'runes of power hidden here; restless through sorcery, to an insidious death, is he who breaks it'. Danish 10th-century stones such as Glavendrup (DR 209) end with 'Þórr vígi …', 'may Thor hallow [these runes / this memorial]', and a curse on anyone who removes the stone.

claims.claim: Runes were used in healing charms.
claims.evidence: The Ribe skull fragment (8th c.) invokes Óðinn and others against pain and a 'dwarf'. The Sigtuna copper amulet (11th c.) is a charm against a 'wolf' of sickness. Many medieval lead amulets carry runic charms. Egils saga ch. 72 describes a healing charm on whalebone, but that is literature, not evidence of practice.

claims.claim: Medieval Christian Scandinavians wrote learned Latin and Hebrew-derived charms in runes (Ave Maria, Pater Noster, the SATOR square, AGLA).
claims.evidence: Such charms appear on runic amulets and on sticks such as the Bryggen finds in Bergen (12th–14th c.). This is where runes meet the Latin magical tradition the rest of the Magical Scriptorium follows. The compiler could not check the individual inscriptions and signa in this run.

claims.claim: Egill Skalla-Grímsson cured a girl by re-carving runes that an unskilled man had cut wrongly on a whalebone.
claims.evidence: Egils saga (written c. 1220–1240), ch. 72 in the Íslenzk fornrit numbering; chapter numbers vary between editions. The saga reports the episode with a skaldic verse attributed to Egill. It shows what 13th-century Icelanders thought about runes, not what 10th-century people did.

claims.claim: Tacitus describes the Germans casting runes for divination.
claims.evidence: Germania 10 (98 CE) describes cutting a branch of a fruit-bearing tree into slips, marking them with 'certain signs' (notis quibusdam), scattering them on a white cloth, and reading three. Tacitus does not say what the signs were. No inscription confirms runic lots, and the earliest runes are about half a century later than Tacitus.

claims.claim: The Elder Futhark has known traditional names and meanings for each rune.
claims.evidence: No Elder Futhark name list survives. The names are reconstructed (asterisked) from the Old English Rune Poem, the Norwegian and Icelandic poems, the Abecedarium Nordmannicum and the Gothic letter names in Vienna, ÖNB Cod. 795. Several are uncertain: *perþ-, *algiz, *kaunan or *kenaz, *laguz or *laukaz. The poems' meanings are medieval and often differ from one another.

claims.claim: The rune poems are magical texts.
claims.evidence: Their form is mnemonic and gnomic: name, then proverb or kenning. The Old English poem is explicitly Christian ('if he wishes to gain glory before the Lord'). Modern occult use treats them as keys to rune meanings, but nothing in them describes magical use.

claims.claim: The 18 Armanen runes were revealed to Guido von List and preserve a lost Aryan priestly wisdom.
claims.evidence: This is List's own claim in Das Geheimnis der Runen (1908): a revelation during his blindness after a 1902 cataract operation. No inscription or manuscript uses this row. It reworks the 16 Younger runes with two invented additions (eh, gibor), keyed to the 18 charms of Hávamál 146–163. Historians (Goodrick-Clarke) treat it as a modern invention within Ariosophy.

claims.claim: The SS and other National Socialist bodies used runes as insignia.
claims.evidence: The doubled Sig-rune of the SS (early 1930s), the Odal rune (SS Race and Settlement Main Office and other units), and the 'life' and 'death' runes (ᛉ upright and inverted) on Lebensborn material and death notices. These uses drew on List's tradition. Since 1945 the German Criminal Code (StGB §86a) has prohibited the public use of symbols of unconstitutional organisations, which covers the SS runes. Today the Odal and 'life' runes also appear in far-right iconography, and the same letters are used without such meaning by historians, by modern Heathen religious groups, and in ordinary Scandinavian use.

claims.claim: The blank 'Odin' rune and the standard modern divinatory meanings are ancient.
claims.evidence: The blank rune first appears in Ralph Blum's The Book of Runes (1982). Divinatory meanings come from 20th-century occult writers working from the medieval rune poems. No ancient source describes divination with individual runes.

claims.claim: erilaz, a title on several early inscriptions ('ek erilaz …'), means 'rune-master' or 'magician'.
claims.evidence: It has been connected to the Heruli, to the jarl rank, and to a professional class of carvers. Its sense is unknown.

claims.claim: Runes were mainly a magical script.
claims.evidence: Against: most of the corpus is memorial stones, ownership and maker's marks, and, at Bryggen, business letters, love notes and jokes. In the 6th century Venantius Fortunatus mentions runes painted on ash tablets as a plain way to send a letter. R. I. Page famously divided runologists into the 'imaginative' and the 'sceptical' and counted himself among the sceptics. For: amuletic formulas, curse stones and healing charms do exist (above). The fair statement is that runes were an ordinary script that was also used for magic.

letters.name: *fehu ('cattle, movable wealth')
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave. On its right, two parallel straight branches slope UP and to the right. The upper branch starts at the top of the stave. The lower one starts about a third of the way down. Each branch reaches out about a third of the stave's height. No curves, no ring-ends. It is the mirror of the a-rune (no. 4), whose branches slope down.
letters.note: It survives into the Younger Futhark and the futhorc with the same sound and the same name, 'wealth', in all three rune poems. Unicode: U+16A0 RUNIC LETTER FEHU FEOH FE F. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER FEHU FEOH FE F

letters.name: *ūruz ('aurochs (wild ox)')
letters.form: An angular inverted U. A full-height stave stands on the left. From its top, a straight stroke slopes down to the right. A second leg, starting lower, about a quarter to a third of the way down, drops vertically or slightly slanted to the baseline. The rune is about half as wide as it is tall. Some early inscriptions round the top.
letters.note: The name differs between the poems. Old English has 'aurochs', the Norwegian poem 'slag', the Icelandic 'drizzle'. *ūruz is a modern reconstruction. Unicode: U+16A2 RUNIC LETTER URUZ UR U. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *þurisaz ('giant (þurs)')
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave with a pointed triangular bow on its right, at mid-height. A straight stroke leaves the stave about a third of the way down and runs down-right to a point about a third of the height out. A second straight stroke returns down-left to the stave about two-thirds down. The stave closes the triangle. Some inscriptions round the bow or set it higher.
letters.note: This is the 'þurs' rune that Skírnir threatens to carve in Skírnismál 36 (see quotations). The Norwegian poem says þurs 'causes the sickness of women', and the Icelandic poem calls it 'the torment of women'. Unicode: U+16A6 RUNIC LETTER THURISAZ THURS THORN. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *ansuz ('a god (one of the Æsir)')
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave. On its right, two parallel straight branches slope DOWN and to the right. The upper branch starts at the top of the stave, the lower about a third of the way down. Each reaches out about a third of the height. It is the mirror of the f-rune's rising branches.
letters.note: In the Anglo-Saxon futhorc this form split into ōs ᚩ, āc ᚪ and æsc ᚫ. In the Younger Futhark the rune stands for a nasal a/o. The Norwegian poem reads óss as 'estuary', the Icelandic poem as 'god'. Unicode: U+16A8 RUNIC LETTER ANSUZ A. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

poemNames.oldEnglish: ōs (the futhorc gives this name to a new rune ᚩ)

letters.name: *raidō ('riding, journey')
letters.form: An angular capital R. A full-height stave. From its top, a straight stroke runs down-right to a point. A second stroke returns down-left to the stave at about mid-height, enclosing a triangular pocket. From that junction, a straight leg runs diagonally down-right to the baseline and ends below the pocket's outer point.
letters.note: Unicode: U+16B1 RUNIC LETTER RAIDO RAD REID R. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER RAIDO RAD REID R

letters.name: *kaunan (or *kenaz) ('ulcer, sore (Norse); torch (Old English)')
letters.form: In the oldest inscriptions it is not full height. It is a small angle like '<': two short straight strokes meet at a point on the left and open to the right. It sits in the upper half of the writing band. Many fonts draw ᚲ at full height. Later forms differ: Anglo-Saxon cēn ᚳ is a stave with two branches falling from its top, and Younger kaun ᚴ is a stave with one branch rising from its middle.
letters.note: Both names, *kaunan and *kenaz, are reconstructions. Handbooks differ on which to print. The Old English and Norse poems give different senses. Unicode: U+16B2 RUNIC LETTER KAUNA. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *gebō ('gift')
letters.form: Two full-height straight diagonals that cross at the centre: an X filling the band. There is no stave.
letters.note: The Younger Futhark dropped it, so there is no Norse rune-poem stanza for it. Unicode: U+16B7 RUNIC LETTER GEBO GYFU G. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *wunjō ('joy')
letters.form: An angular P. A full-height stave with a closed triangular flag on its upper right. A straight stroke runs from the stave's top down-right to a point. A second returns down-left to the stave between a third and half of the way down.
letters.note: The Anglo-Saxon wynn passed into Old English book-hand as the letter ƿ (wynn), which scribes used for w. Unicode: U+16B9 RUNIC LETTER WUNJO WYNN W. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *hagalaz ('hail')
letters.form: Two parallel full-height staves joined by one straight crossbar. The bar runs diagonally from the upper part of the left stave down to the lower part of the right stave. Continental and Anglo-Saxon inscriptions often have two parallel crossbars instead (ᚻ, U+16BB, 'haegl'). The Younger Futhark has the different forms ᚼ and ᚽ.
letters.note: Which form appears where is the compiler's recollection of the handbooks (single bar in Scandinavia, double bar on the continent and in England); check it against Barnes 2012 or Düwel 2008. Unicode: U+16BA RUNIC LETTER HAGLAZ H. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *naudiz ('need, constraint')
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave crossed at mid-height by one short straight stroke that slopes down from left to right. The stroke projects a little on both sides of the stave.
letters.note: Sigrdrífumál 7 tells the reader to mark 'Nauð' on the fingernail as an ale-rune (see quotations). Unicode: U+16BE RUNIC LETTER NAUDIZ NYD NAUD N. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER NAUDIZ NYD NAUD N

letters.name: *īsaz ('ice')
letters.form: A single full-height vertical stave.
letters.note: Unicode: U+16C1 RUNIC LETTER ISAZ IS ISS I. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER ISAZ IS ISS I

letters.name: *jēra ('year, (good) harvest')
letters.form: The standard (Unicode) form: two separate angular hooks set on a diagonal. Each hook is two short straight strokes meeting at an angle. One sits upper-left, the other lower-right. Each opens towards the other. They overlap in height across the middle of the band but do not touch. Early inscriptions vary more on this rune than on any other: some put a stave through the middle, some round the hooks.
letters.note: Old j became a in the Younger Futhark (ár), because Proto-Norse lost initial j-, so *jāra became ár. The Anglo-Saxon gēr has its own form ᛄ (U+16C4). Unicode: U+16C3 RUNIC LETTER JERAN J. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *ī(h)waz / *eihwaz ('yew')
letters.value: Ï (a vowel near i or e; value disputed)
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave. A short straight stroke runs from its top, slanting down to the right, about a fifth of the height. A matching stroke runs from its foot, slanting up to the left. The figure is point-symmetric, like a stretched S or Z on a vertical spine. Mirror forms also occur, with the top branch to the left.
letters.note: Its sound value is one of the open questions of runology. The yew name passed to a different rune in the Younger Futhark (see no. 15). Unicode: U+16C7 RUNIC LETTER IWAZ EOH. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

poemNames.norwegian: (dropped; the Younger yew-name ýr went to the z/R-rune)

letters.name: *perþ- (meaning unknown) ('unknown')
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave with two open angles on its right, one at the top and one at the foot, like a cup lying on its side and opening to the right. From the stave's top, a short straight stroke runs down-right, then turns straight down for a short distance. From the stave's foot, a mirror stroke runs up-right, then turns straight up. The two short ends do not meet, so the right side is open across the middle.
letters.note: It is the rarest rune of the row and is almost absent from early inscriptions. The meaning of peorð is unknown (guesses include a dice-cup, a pear tree or a game). Draw from the Noto Sans Runic glyph and check against Kylver; the compiler is less sure of the exact angles here than for the common runes. Unicode: U+16C8 RUNIC LETTER PERTHO PEORTH P. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *algiz (reconstruction uncertain) ('elk? protection?')
letters.value: Z, later R (final -z of Proto-Germanic, later a palatal r)
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave. Two straight branches spring from it between half and two-thirds of the way up. They rise diagonally up-left and up-right and end about level with the stave's top: an upward fork like a trident or Greek psi. Some Elder inscriptions invert it, with the branches pointing down. The inverted form became standard as Younger ýr ᛦ (U+16E6).
letters.note: This is the rune modern writers call the 'life rune' (Lebensrune). As a symbol it was used in National Socialist Germany, e.g. by the Lebensborn organisation and on death notices; see claims and cautions. The rune poems do not support a reading as 'protection'. Unicode: U+16C9 RUNIC LETTER ALGIZ EOLHX. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *sōwilō ('sun')
letters.form: A vertical zigzag of straight strokes, like a lightning flash. In the standard form there are three strokes: a short steep stroke, a longer diagonal running back across, and a second short steep stroke, alternating direction from top to bottom. Inscriptions have from three to about eight strokes, in either orientation.
letters.note: Copy the exact orientation from the Noto Sans Runic glyph; inscriptions vary too much for one 'correct' drawing. The doubled 'Sig rune' of the SS was drawn from this rune (see claims). In the Younger Futhark the s-rune is ᛋ (long-branch) or ᛌ (short-twig). Unicode: U+16CA RUNIC LETTER SOWILO S. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *tīwaz ('the god Tiw / Týr')
letters.form: An upward arrow. A full-height stave with two short straight strokes falling from its top, one to the left and one to the right. They reach down a quarter to a third of the height.
letters.note: Sigrdrífumál 6 says victory-runes are carved on the sword-hilt, 'naming Týr twice'. Many scholars connect that line to this rune. Unicode: U+16CF RUNIC LETTER TIWAZ TIR TYR T. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER TIWAZ TIR TYR T

poemNames.oldEnglish: Tīr (in the poem, a guiding star or sign)
poemNames.icelandic: Týr ('the one-handed god'; Latin gloss Mars)

letters.name: *berkanan ('birch (twig)')
letters.form: An angular capital B. A full-height stave with two closed triangular bows on its right, one above the other. Two straight strokes go out from the stave's top to a point and back to its middle. Two more go out from the middle to a point and back to the foot. Early forms sometimes separate the bows slightly or round them.
letters.note: Unicode: U+16D2 RUNIC LETTER BERKANAN BEORC BJARKAN B. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER BERKANAN BEORC BJARKAN B

letters.name: *ehwaz ('horse')
letters.form: An angular M with a shallow middle. Two parallel full-height staves. A straight stroke runs from the top of the left stave down-right to a point midway between them, about a third of the height down. A second rises from that point to the top of the right stave. The middle V does not reach the baseline.
letters.note: Unicode: U+16D6 RUNIC LETTER EHWAZ EH E. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *mannaz ('man, human being')
letters.form: Two parallel full-height staves with two straight diagonals crossing between them in the upper half. One runs from the top of the left stave to about mid-height on the right stave. The other runs from the top of the right stave to about mid-height on the left. Together they make an X between the staves.
letters.note: The Younger Futhark m is a different form: ᛘ (long-branch) or ᛙ (short-twig). Unicode: U+16D7 RUNIC LETTER MANNAZ MAN M. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *laguz (or *laukaz) ('water, lake (or leek)')
letters.form: A full-height vertical stave with one short straight branch. It leaves the top of the stave and slopes down to the right for about a third of the height.
letters.note: Some runologists reconstruct the Elder name as *laukaz 'leek', not *laguz 'water', because laukaz is a common word on bracteates. This is a disputed proposal. The rune poems all give the 'water' name. Unicode: U+16DA RUNIC LETTER LAUKAZ LAGU LOGR L. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.
letters.unicodeName: RUNIC LETTER LAUKAZ LAGU LOGR L

letters.name: *ingwaz ('the god Ing (Yngvi)')
letters.form: A closed square standing on one corner (a diamond, ◇). It is usually smaller than the other runes and set in the upper part or middle of the band. Some inscriptions draw it full height or put it on a stave. The Anglo-Saxon form ᛝ (U+16DD) is a diamond whose sides run on into crossing tails.
letters.note: Size and position vary between the early rows. The compiler could not check Kylver's form in this run. Unicode: U+16DC RUNIC LETTER INGWAZ. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

poemNames.oldEnglish: Ing (a hero or god 'first seen among the East Danes')

letters.name: *dagaz ('day')
letters.form: Two parallel full-height staves joined by two straight diagonals that cross at the centre. One runs from the top of the left stave to the foot of the right stave, the other from the top of the right stave to the foot of the left. The result looks like an hourglass lying on its side, closed by the two staves.
letters.note: On Kylver, d comes before o. On some bracteate rows and in the Old English poem it comes after o (ēþel, then dæg). Unicode: U+16DE RUNIC LETTER DAGAZ DAEG D. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

letters.name: *ōþalan / *ōþila ('inherited land, ancestral estate')
letters.form: A diamond (a square on its corner) filling the upper two-thirds of the band. Its two lower sides run on past the bottom corner, cross there, and continue as two short legs splayed down-left and down-right to the baseline. There is no stave.
letters.note: This is the 'odal rune'. In National Socialist Germany a variant was used by the SS Race and Settlement Main Office and by other units. A variant with serifs or 'wings' appears in post-war far-right iconography. The plain letter form above is the historical one. Do not print the winged variant. Unicode: U+16DF RUNIC LETTER OTHALAN ETHEL O. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions (asterisked). Only the Old English, Norwegian and Icelandic rune-poem names are attested.

lettersSource: The Elder Futhark, 24 runes in three ættir of eight, in the conventional modern order of the handbooks (Barnes 2012; Düwel 2008). That order follows the Grumpan and Vadstena bracteates for … i j ï p z … and Kylver for the ending … ŋ d o. Some editions print … ŋ o d, as in the Old English poem's ēþel–dæg. Characters, code points and Unicode names come from the Runic block U+16A0–U+16FF, checked in this session against the Unicode Character Database 14.0 (Python unicodedata). The glyphs should be set in Noto Sans Runic (@fontsource/noto-sans-runic 5.3.0, runic subset U+16A0–16F8; see understand.md §7), not drawn. The 'form' fields describe the normalised printed forms of the handbooks and Unicode charts, with the main inscriptional variants, so the page can explain a shape or check the font. The forms were not traced from any single inscription. Rune-poem names follow Dickins 1915 and Halsall 1981. Proto-Germanic names are modern reconstructions. Runes have no numerical values in the early tradition, so numeric is null. Supporting rows are given under youngerFuthark, futhorcAdditions and armanenRow (the last for the 'modern invention' panel only).

armanenRow.note: Guido von List's 1908 row of 18, as listed in Goodrick-Clarke 1985 and in the Flowers translation. Show it as a modern invention, with names only. Do not draw it with the SS or other organisational stylings.

uses.use: Everyday writing: memorials, ownership and maker's marks, letters and messages
uses.evidence: This is the bulk of the corpus. Viking-Age memorial stones in Sweden, Denmark and Norway; the Bryggen sticks of Bergen (12th–14th c.); and Venantius Fortunatus, Carmina VII.18 (6th c.), on runes painted on ash tablets for letters.
Words such as alu, laþu, laukaz, auja ('luck') and gibu auja ('I give luck') on 5th–6th-century gold bracteates and other objects. The sense is disputed (see claims).
Björketorp and Stentoften (Blekinge, 6th–7th c.); Danish 'Þórr vígi' stones such as Glavendrup (10th c.).
The Ribe skull fragment (8th c.); the Sigtuna amulet (11th c.); medieval lead amulets; and, in literature, Egils saga ch. 72.

uses.use: Christian and learned charms written in runes
uses.evidence: Latin prayers, the SATOR square and AGLA on medieval runic amulets and sticks (MacLeod & Mees 2006). This is the overlap with the Latin and Hebrew magical traditions of the rest of the wing.

uses.use: Eddic 'rune-craft': victory, ale, birth, sea, limb, speech and mind runes
uses.evidence: Sigrdrífumál 6–13 names each kind and where to carve it. Stanza 18 (by the compiler's count) says the runes were shaved off and mixed into the holy mead, the same scraping-off Egill performs. Hávamál 144 asks whether the reader knows how to carve (rísta), interpret (ráða), stain (fá), test (freista), ask, sacrifice, send and slay. This is literary and late, but it is the main textual source for a magical understanding of runes.

uses.use: Mnemonic and poetic use of the rune names
uses.evidence: The three rune poems; Cynewulf's runic signatures; Old English riddles that use runes.
The cipher runes on the Rök stone (early 9th c.), and the medieval Icelandic and Scandinavian traditions of coded runes built on the three ættir.

Medieval and early modern perpetual calendars on staves and boards use the 16 Younger runes plus three extra signs (arlaug, tvímaðr, belgþor) for the 19 golden numbers. Unicode encodes these as U+16EE–U+16F0.

There is no ancient evidence for divination with individual runes. Tacitus's lots (Germania 10) carried unspecified signs. Present-day rune casting comes from 20th-century writers, especially List (1908) and Blum (1982).

uses.use: Early modern learned esotericism and modern occultism
uses.evidence: Johannes Bureus's Adulruna (17th c.); List's Armanen runes (1908) and the völkisch rune-occultists of the 1920s–30s; post-war Heathen and occult use (reported only, not reproduced).

quotations.text: Veit ek, at ek hekk / vindga meiði á / nætr allar níu, / geiri undaðr / ok gefinn Óðni, / sjálfr sjálfum mér, / á þeim meiði, / er manngi veit / hvers af rótum renn.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse (normalised spelling as in Neckel–Kuhn). Henry Adams Bellows, The Poetic Edda (American-Scandinavian Foundation, 1923; public domain), where it is stanza 139: "I ween that I hung | on the windy tree, / Hung there for nights full nine; / With the spear I was wounded, | and offered I was / To Othin, myself to myself, / On the tree that none | may ever know / What root beneath it runs." The Bellows wording is quoted from memory: check it against the 1923 printing before use.

quotations.text: Við hleifi mik sældu / né við hornigi; / nýsta ek niðr, / nam ek upp rúnar, / æpandi nam, / fell ek aptr þaðan.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse. Bellows 1923, stanza 140: "None made me happy | with loaf or horn, / And there below I looked; / I took up the runes, | shrieking I took them, / And forthwith back I fell." Quoted from memory; check against the printing.

quotations.text: Þat er þá reynt, / er þú at rúnum spyrr / inum reginkunnum, / þeim er gerðu ginnregin / ok fáði fimbulþulr.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase, not a published translation: 'It is proven, when you ask about the runes of divine descent, which the mighty powers made and the great sage coloured [painted].'

quotations.text: Veiztu hvé rísta skal? / Veiztu hvé ráða skal? / Veiztu hvé fá skal? / Veiztu hvé freista skal? / Veiztu hvé biðja skal? / Veiztu hvé blóta skal? / Veiztu hvé senda skal? / Veiztu hvé sóa skal?
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'Do you know how to carve? how to read [interpret]? how to colour? how to test? how to ask? how to offer? how to send? how to slaughter [sacrifice]?'

quotations.text: Sigrúnar skaltu kunna, / ef þú vilt sigr hafa, / ok rísta á hjalti hjǫrs, / sumar á véttrimum, / sumar á valbǫstum, / ok nefna tvisvar Tý.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'Victory-runes you must know if you want victory, and carve them on the sword's hilt, some on the blade-guards, some on the blade, and name Týr twice.' The two blade terms are of uncertain meaning.

quotations.text: Ǫlrúnar skaltu kunna, / ef þú vill annars kvæn / véli-t þik í tryggð, ef þú trúir; / á horni skal þær rísta / ok á handar baki / ok merkja á nagli Nauð.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'Ale-runes you must know if you do not want another man's wife to betray your trust; carve them on the horn and on the back of the hand, and mark Nauð [the n-rune] on the nail.'

quotations.text: Full skal signa / ok við fári sjá / ok verpa lauk í lǫg.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'The cup must be blessed, and guarded against harm, and a leek thrown into the liquid.' This is the literary parallel to laukaz on the bracteates.

quotations.text: Þurs ríst ek þér / ok þrjá stafi, / ergi ok æði / ok óþola; / svá ek þat af ríst, / sem ek þat á reist, / ef gørask þarfar þess.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'A þurs [the þ-rune] I carve for you, and three staves: lust and frenzy and unbearable longing. I can carve it off as I carved it on, if there is need.'

quotations.text: Skalat maðr rúnar rísta, / nema ráða vel kunni; / þat verðr mǫrgum manni, / es of myrkvan staf villisk; / sák á telgðu talkni / tíu launstafi ristna; / þat hefr lauka lindi / langs ofrtrega fengit.
quotations.translation: Original Old Norse with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'A man should not carve runes unless he can read them well; many a man goes astray over a dark letter. I saw ten secret staves carved on the whittled whalebone; they have brought the linden of leeks [the woman] long, heavy grief.' Published translations: Hermann Pálsson & Paul Edwards (Penguin Classics, 1976); Bernard Scudder, in The Complete Sagas of Icelanders I (1997).
quotations.source: Egils saga Skalla-Grímssonar, ch. 72 (Íslenzk fornrit II, ed. Sigurður Nordal, 1933); chapter number to verify

quotations.text: virgam frugiferae arbori decisam in surculos amputant eosque notis quibusdam discretos super candidam vestem temere ac fortuito spargunt.
quotations.translation: Original Latin with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'They cut a branch from a fruit-bearing tree into slips, mark them with certain signs, and scatter them at random over a white cloth.' The signs are not said to be runes. A published English version: M. Hutton, revised E. H. Warmington, Loeb Classical Library (1970).

quotations.text: barbara fraxineis pingatur runa tabellis, / quodque papyrus agit, virgula plana valet.
quotations.translation: Original Latin with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'Let the barbarian rune be painted on tablets of ash; what papyrus does, a smoothed stick can do.' Evidence for runes as an ordinary means of correspondence.
quotations.source: Venantius Fortunatus, Carmina VII.18 (to Flavus), 6th c.

quotations.text: Feoh byþ frofur fira gehwylcum; / sceal ðeah manna gehwylc miclun hyt dælan / gif he wile for drihtne domes hleotan.
quotations.translation: Bruce Dickins, Runic and Heroic Poems of the Old Teutonic Peoples (Cambridge UP, 1915): 'Wealth is a comfort to all men; yet must every man bestow it freely, if he wish to gain honour in the sight of the Lord.' Quoted from memory; check against the printing.
quotations.source: Old English Rune Poem, stanza 1 (feoh); text from Hickes's Thesaurus, 1703–05

quotations.text: Fé vældr frænda róge; / føðesk ulfr í skóge.
quotations.translation: Dickins 1915: 'Wealth is a source of discord among kinsmen; the wolf lives in the forest.' Quoted from memory; check against the printing.

quotations.text: Fé er frænda róg / ok flæðar viti / ok grafseiðs gata. aurum. fylkir.
quotations.translation: Dickins 1915: 'Wealth: source of discord among kinsmen and fire of the sea and path of the serpent.' Quoted from memory; check against the printing.
Proto-Norse original as transliterated in the handbooks, with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'I paint (write) the rune derived from the gods.'

quotations.text: izwis atgiban ist kunnan runa þiudangardjos gudis
quotations.translation: Gothic original with the compiler's own paraphrase: 'to you it is given to know the mystery (runa) of the kingdom of God.' It shows rūna = Greek mystērion.

links.relation: One of the three candidate parents (Wimmer 1874). Medieval Scandinavians also wrote Latin prayers and charms in runes, and Ole Worm and Bureus made rune study part of Latin learning.
Another proposed parent (Bugge; von Friesen), now generally rejected on chronology. Gothic rūna translates Greek mystērion.
The remote ancestor, through Greek and the Etruscan or North Italic alphabets.

AGLA, a notarikon of Hebrew 'Atah gibbor le-olam Adonai', appears on medieval runic amulets, and Bureus's Adulruna drew on Christian Kabbalah. This is where the runic tradition meets the Hebrew-based magical alphabets.

Both appear in modern 'magical alphabet' lists and in modern witchcraft, but they have unrelated histories: Theban is a learned 1518 alphabet keyed to Latin; runes are a native script. Do not present them as one tradition.

To check, not to assert: the compiler believes the Carolingian De inventione litterarum, attributed to Hrabanus Maurus, gives a runic alphabet 'of the Northmen', and that Trithemius's Polygraphia (1518) may print a 'Norman' alphabet descended from it. This could not be verified in this run.

Contrast only. Icelandic galdrastafir (magical staves, e.g. in the 16th–17th-century Galdrabók and the 19th-century Huld manuscript) are sign-magic like the charaktêres and are not runes, although they sometimes include runes. The 'vegvísir' and 'ægishjálmur' come from those late manuscripts, not from the Viking Age.

cautions: No web search was possible for this item: the run's shared search budget was used up before it started. This rests on the compiler's background knowledge of the named work, not on a page read for this brief. Check it against the named edition before publication. This applies to every date, edition, stanza, chapter, signum and quotation wording in this file. The Unicode code points and names are the exception: they were checked mechanically in this session.

Stanza and chapter numbers differ between editions. Hávamál 138 in Neckel–Kuhn and Larrington is 139 in Bellows (to verify). Egils saga chapter numbers differ between Íslenzk fornrit and the translations. Always cite the edition.
Mark the Proto-Germanic names (*fehu, *ansuz …) as reconstructions on the page. Only the rune-poem and manuscript names are attested, and those are medieval.
Do not present the modern divinatory meanings, the blank rune, the 'Armanen' row, 'rune yoga' or the vegvísir as ancient. Report them under 'modern', with dates.

Sensitive symbols: the doubled Sig-rune, the Odal rune with 'wings' or serifs, the 'life/death' runes in SS styling, and the Wolfsangel (not a rune) are prohibited in some contexts in Germany (StGB §86a) and appear in hate-symbol databases. Show runes only as letters in their historical rows, in a neutral typeface. Report the Nazi-era use soberly and in its own section. Do not reproduce insignia.

Do not reproduce the emblems or texts of living organisations: modern Heathen bodies such as Ásatrúarfélagið (recognised in Iceland since 1973), or rune-occult orders. They may be named, but not illustrated.

The Codex Regius poems (c. 1270) and Egils saga (c. 1220–40) were written in Christian Iceland, centuries after the Elder Futhark went out of use. They are evidence for medieval ideas about runes, not for Migration-Period practice.

Agrippa does not print runes among the alphabets of De occulta philosophia III.29–30 (the compiler's recollection, to verify). The runes enter the learned-magic lineage only through Bureus (17th c.) and the medieval Latin charms written in runes, so the wing should not imply an Agrippan pedigree.

Stephen E. Flowers (Runes and Magic, 1986) is an academic runologist who also writes on rune occultism as Edred Thorsson. Cite his dissertation for formula data, and pair it with sceptical runologists (Page, Barnes) on interpretation.
Wikipedia, Omniglot and rune-divination sites are not sources for history here. The Unicode chart is a source for code points only.
